memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "'Anyone, whether native-born or foreigner, who eats anything found dead or torn by wild animals must wash their clothes and bathe with water, and they will be ceremonially unclean till evening; then they will be clean. But if they do not wash their clothes and bathe themselves, they will be held responsible.'" - Lev 17:15-16 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
The chapter ends not with a threat but with a provision.

Someone eats an animal found dead — perhaps out of hunger, perhaps without knowing. It makes them unclean. And immediately God gives the remedy: wash, wait until evening, and you will be clean.

The failure is not final. There is a way back.

But read the last verse carefully. Judgement falls on the one who does not wash. Not on the person who became unclean — on the person who refused the cleansing that was freely available.

That distinction runs through the whole Bible. Our sin is not what finally condemns us; Christ has dealt with sin. What condemns is refusing the remedy God has provided. This is the verdict: light has come into the world, but people loved darkness (John 3:19).

There is no sin so great that Christ's blood cannot cleanse it. But the cleansing has to be received. A remedy left on the shelf heals no one.

So the question at the end of Leviticus 17 is a simple one, and it is the same question the gospel asks. God has provided the way. Will you take it?

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Is there something you have not brought to God for cleansing?
2. What stops you from receiving what He freely offers?
3. Have you personally received the forgiveness Christ purchased?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, thank You that You never leave me without a way back. I refuse to leave Your remedy untouched — wash me, forgive me, and make me clean through Christ. Amen.
